title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 33: Hernandez v. Napocor: Injunction Against High-Voltage Lines Adjacent to Residences
primary_topics: Chapter 33 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Hernandez v. Napocor, in which a unanimous Supreme Court, through Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario, held that Presidential Decree 1818 did not bar a trial court from enjoining the energizing of Napocor's 230-kilovolt transmission line through a residential village.

The reading that saved the injunction: the prohibition in PD 1818 reaches only injunctions against administrative acts involving facts or the exercise of discretion in technical cases, and not controversies raising questions of law such as the right to health and the Local Government Code's prior-consultation requirement.

The evidentiary standard for a provisional remedy: probability, not certainty, suffices for a preliminary injunction under Section 3 of Rule 58, and the record -- studies linking electromagnetic fields to cancer and leukemia, Napocor's own brochure on safe distances, and its negotiations offering four relocation options -- engendered a cloud of doubt over the project's danger.

The value ordering the Court announced: infrastructure and economic development matter, but the primordial concern is the far-reaching irreversible effect on human safety, health and the preservation of life itself in all of its desired quality.
sub_topics: The facts: from 1996 Napocor built 29 steel poles, each 53.4 meters high, for its 230-kilovolt Sucat-Araneta-Balintawak Power Transmission Project, carrying overhead tension cables through Dasmarinas Village, Makati City, where petitioners lived.

The alarm: petitioners found scientific studies that electromagnetic fields from high-voltage lines could cause illnesses from cancer to leukemia, Representative Francis Joseph G. Escudero denounced Napocor's cavalier disregard of safety and consultation requirements in a privileged speech, and Representative Arnulfo Fuentebella demanded an explanation.

The impasse: Napocor admitted it was still negotiating and had four options -- transfer the line, keep a 12-meter distance from the village, build an underground line, or reroute along C-5 and the South Luzon Expressway -- but the negotiations failed.

The litigation: petitioners filed a Complaint for Damages with a prayer for a TRO on March 9, 2000; Judge Francisco B. Ibay restrained the energizing of the line; Napocor went to the Court of Appeals on certiorari invoking Section 1 of Presidential Decree 1818, which strips courts of jurisdiction to enjoin government infrastructure projects.

The Court of Appeals reversed on May 3, 2000, holding that PD 1818 clearly proscribed injunctions against infrastructure projects and citing Supreme Court Circulars 2-91 and 13-93; petitioners argued to the Supreme Court that the proscription should not apply to cases of extreme urgency where health and safety hang in the balance.

The ruling: PD 1818 aimed only to avert the untimely frustration of government infrastructure projects by provisional remedies and was not meant to be a blanket prohibition disregarding a community's fundamental right to health, safety and well-being; the prohibition covers administrative acts involving facts or technical discretion, not questions of law.

Why this case raised questions of law: petitioners put in issue the violation of their constitutionally protected right to health and Napocor's compliance with the Local Government Code provision on prior consultation with affected communities, which removed the case from the protective mantle of PD 1818.

The three evidentiary props for the injunction: the studies linking illness to electromagnetic fields; Napocor's own Quezon power project brochure requiring safe distances from residences; and the documented negotiations and relocation options, which showed the health concerns were far from imaginary.

The probability standard: although the safety of the lines was ultimately evidentiary and went to the merits, the health risk lay within the realm of a scientific scale of probability, and probability is enough for an injunction to issue as a provisional remedy, injunction as a main action being the remedy that demands absolute certainty.

The circulars clarified: Circulars 2-91 and 13-93 did not impose an unbridled prohibition but enjoined judges to observe utmost caution, prudence and judiciousness, and so did not tie the hands of courts.

The closing balance: the Decision did not seek to undermine a project aimed at the common good, but held that human safety outweighed presumed economic benefits, asking of what use modernization would be if it proved a scourge to an individual's fundamental right to life in all of its desired quality.

notable_anecdotes: The village under the wires: 29 steel poles, each 53.4 meters high, were rising to carry 230-kilovolt cables directly over the Dasmarinas Village homes of the petitioners.

Trouble ensued when residents discovered scientific studies linking electromagnetic fields from high-voltage lines to illnesses from cancer to leukemia, and the dispute moved from the village to the floor of Congress.
Napocor's own words used against it: the Court noted that the company's brochure on its Quezon power project itself required power lines to be located at safe distances from residences.

The four options as evidence of concern: the Court reasoned that if there had truly been no cause for alarm, Napocor would not have offered to transfer, distance, bury or reroute the line, nor would Representative Escudero have fired away strong words of censure.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 33 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Hernandez v. Napocor, decided unanimously through Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario. From 1996 the National Power Corporation erected 29 steel poles, each 53.4 meters high, to carry the overhead cables of its 230-kilovolt Sucat-Araneta-Balintawak Power Transmission Project through Dasmarinas Village in Makati, where the petitioners lived. Trouble followed when residents found scientific studies linking the electromagnetic fields of high-voltage lines to illnesses ranging from cancer to leukemia; Representative Francis Joseph G. Escudero denounced Napocor's cavalier treatment of safety and consultation requirements in a privileged speech, Representative Arnulfo Fuentebella demanded an explanation, and Napocor's four options -- transferring the line, keeping a 12-meter distance, going underground, or rerouting along C-5 and the South Luzon Expressway -- ended in impasse. Petitioners sued for damages with a prayer for a restraining order in March 2000, Judge Francisco B. Ibay restrained the energizing of the line, and the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Section 1 of Presidential Decree 1818 stripped courts of jurisdiction to enjoin government infrastructure projects. The Supreme Court granted the petition. It held that PD 1818 aimed only to avert the untimely frustration of government infrastructure projects and was never meant to be a blanket prohibition that would disregard the fundamental right to the health, safety and well-being of a community; the bar covered administrative acts involving facts or technical discretion, not questions of law, and this case raised questions of law -- the constitutional right to health and Napocor's compliance with the Local Government Code's prior-consultation requirement. The injunction also found support in Section 3 of Rule 58, which requires only a probable violation of rights, and the record -- the studies, Napocor's own brochure requiring safe distances from residences, and its documented relocation negotiations -- placed the risk within the realm of a scientific scale of probability, which was enough for a provisional remedy. The Court added that its circulars enjoined utmost caution, prudence and judiciousness rather than an unbridled prohibition, and closed by asking of what use modernization would be if it proved a scourge to an individual's fundamental right to life in all of its desired quality.
